facts: Code actions are the riskiest v1 item and are deliberately built LAST (docs/design/tool-surface.md#Build-order item 7, accepted in loop/design-approval.json's sequencing decision) — it is the only tool with server-side state, a two-phase protocol, and the widest JDT LS surface. Every other v1 tool is already shippable without it, so if v1 must slip anything, it slips this.

JDT LS returns code actions UNRESOLVED: edit:undefined, command:undefined, data:<opaque> (spike D). A second codeAction/resolve round-trip fills in the edit. Observed titles on a trivial file: 'Organize imports', "Add @SuppressWarnings 'unused' to 'Unused'", 'Generate toString()', 'Change modifiers to final where possible'.

The daemon holds JDT LS's opaque 'data' blob server-side and hands the CALLER an opaque actionId instead — there is no value in round-tripping JDT LS's internal blob through an LLM's context window, and doing so would also leak an implementation detail the caller cannot use (INV-CA-2: 'every actionId handed out is either resolvable or expired-with-an-error; a handle never resolves to an edit belonging to a different action').

The handle is a STALENESS HAZARD by construction: a handle minted before an edit and resolved after it would apply an edit computed against source that no longer exists. INV-CA-1 requires the resolve step to check the workspace's sync generation (owned by feat-file-sync-watcher) at mint time against the generation at resolve time, and error on any mismatch — never silently resolve against stale source.

A-002 (verified, human-confirmed 2026-08-19): mutating tools return the proposed edit as data by default; apply:true is opt-in per call. This applies to java_apply_code_action exactly as it does to java_rename (INV-TOOL-2) — the code-action-specific invariants (INV-CA-1, INV-CA-2) are about handle validity, not about the write-vs-return decision, which is a separate, already-settled concern.

Both java_code_actions (mints handles) and java_apply_code_action (resolves them) share this one packet because the staleness hazard spans both — implementing one without the other in mind produces a handle table with no real invalidation path.
